prompt: In the `TwoApis` transcript, why does the Options card say `(1 requests)` and the Composition card `(0 requests)`?
hint: Which of the two values is shared, and which is each card's own?

choices.text: The Composition card's `ref` did not redraw its template
choices.why: It did redraw: its percentage moved to 33% with the other. Its count is 0 because nobody pressed its button.

choices.text: Only one card may count requests while they share `done`
choices.why: Sharing `done` says nothing about `clicks`. Press the second button and it counts too.

choices.text: Each card has its own `clicks`, and one was pressed
choices.why: Right. `done` lives in `TwoApis` and both read it; `clicks` is state of each card, and only the first was clicked.

choices.text: The Options card counted one click in `data` and its `emit` counted none
choices.why: There is one count per card and it lives in `data`; the emit only told the parent to add 15 minutes.

prompt: In the `TwoApis` transcript, what percentage did both cards show after the click?
hint: 60 of 180, rounded.

prompt: A component of five hundred lines does four things in the Options API. What does changing one of those things involve?
hint: The second row of the table: what is the code grouped by?

choices.text: One entry in `methods`, since each concern is one method
choices.why: A concern has state, derived values, a watcher and cleanup too, and those live in other options.

choices.text: A rewrite into `<script setup>` before anything can change
choices.why: Options components keep working and can be changed in place; the last section moves one across a piece at a time.

choices.text: One mixin, because Options code keeps each concern in a mixin of its own
choices.why: Mixins are a way to share options between components, not how a single component is laid out.

choices.text: Visits to `data`, `computed`, `watch` and `beforeUnmount`
choices.why: Right. The code is grouped by kind, so one concern's pieces sit in four options, far apart.

prompt: Why is `data` written as a function that returns an object, rather than as the object itself?
hint: How many cards would hold the same `clicks`?

choices.text: Each instance calls it and gets a fresh object
choices.why: Right. Vue calls it once per instance; one shared object would give every card the same `clicks`.

choices.text: Vue 3 cannot make a plain object reactive
choices.why: It can: `reactive({})` does exactly that. The function is about how many objects there are, not whether they react.

choices.text: So Vue can wait to build the state until the template first reads it
choices.why: Vue calls `data()` while the instance is created, before `created`, whatever the template reads.

choices.text: So that `this` inside it is the parent component
choices.why: `this` in an option is the component's own instance; the function is there to make a new object per instance.

prompt: In an Options API component, which of these can `this.label` be? Choose all that apply.
hint: Vue merges several options onto one object.

choices.text: A prop
choices.why: Right. Props are on `this` beside everything else.

choices.text: A ref that you read as `this.label.value`
choices.why: On `this` a ref is unwrapped: `this.label` is already the value.

choices.text: A computed value
choices.why: Right. Computed values join `this` as well, read without calling them.

choices.text: A property that a mixin's `data` added
choices.why: Right. That is why nothing says where a name came from: a mixin can put it there too.

choices.text: A `const` declared inside another method
choices.why: A local constant belongs to the call of that method and never reaches the instance.

choices.text: A data property
choices.why: Right. `data()` returns the state, and each key of it is on `this`.

prompt: `this.clicks` is the value, not a ref. Which cost of that does the lesson name?
hint: Think of a function that should keep following a value after it was called.

choices.text: Every read needs `.value`, and it is easy to forget
choices.why: That is the Composition API's cost, the other way round: on `this` there is no `.value` to forget.

choices.text: There is no ref to hand to a function that should follow it
choices.why: Right. You can only pass the current number; lesson 2's rules needed the ref itself to keep tracking.

choices.text: The template no longer updates when `clicks` changes
choices.why: It does: the card redrew `(1 requests)`. Unwrapping changes how you read the value, not whether it reacts.

choices.text: Vue copies the number on every read, which slows a large component down
choices.why: Nothing is copied; `this.clicks` reads through to the reactive state each time.

prompt: In `ThisTrap`, why did `Shorter` throw while `Longer` worked?
hint: Read the error: what was `this` when `minutes` was read?

choices.text: Its `this` was `window`, which has no `minutes`
choices.why: Then the read would give `undefined`, not throw. The error reads a property of `undefined`: in a module the top-level `this` is `undefined`.

choices.text: Vue binds methods in order and stopped after the first
choices.why: Vue binds every method; binding an arrow simply has no effect, because an arrow keeps the `this` it was written with.

choices.text: It is an arrow, and its `this` is the module's: `undefined`
choices.why: Right. An arrow ignores how it is called; its `this` was fixed when the module was evaluated.

choices.text: A method may not subtract from `data`; only a computed can change it
choices.why: `longer` changed `data` from a method a moment earlier. Computed values derive, they do not write.

prompt: In the `ThisTrap` transcript, how many minutes did the page show after both clicks?
hint: Only one of the two buttons did its job.

prompt: A method contains `setTimeout(function () { this.minutes += 15 }, 1000)`. What happens to the component's `minutes`?
hint: The callback is an ordinary function. Who calls it?

choices.text: It goes up by 15, because Vue binds every function written inside a method
choices.why: Vue binds the method itself, not the functions it creates; this one gets its `this` from the timer.

choices.text: Nothing: the callback's `this` is set by the timer
choices.why: Right. An ordinary function has a `this` of its own, and the timer's is not the component. An arrow would have kept the method's.

choices.text: It goes up by 15 only if the method is written as an arrow too
choices.why: An arrow method has the module's `this`, `undefined`, so the arrow inside it would inherit `undefined` as well.

choices.text: The component fails to load: `function` is refused inside `methods`
choices.why: Vue never sees the inner function; it is ordinary JavaScript and runs, with the wrong `this`.

prompt: In `OptionsLifecycle`, why did `beforeCreate` print `minutes is undefined`?
hint: Compare it with the line `created` printed.

choices.text: `minutes` is in `data`, and only `props` exist that early
choices.why: Props are set up before this hook, but that is beside the point: `minutes` is data, and data comes later.

choices.text: `data` had not been set up yet
choices.why: Right. The instance existed and its state did not; by `created`, one step later, `minutes` was 30.

choices.text: `this` inside a hook is not the component
choices.why: A hook written as a method has the component as `this`; `created` read `minutes` through it a moment later.

choices.text: The template had not drawn `minutes` on the page yet
choices.why: Rendering has nothing to do with the value: `created` read 30 with nothing rendered.

prompt: Why did `mounted` print `the element is a #text`?
hint: Count the roots of the template.

choices.text: `mounted` runs before the DOM exists, so `$el` is a placeholder
choices.why: The DOM exists by `mounted`; `created` was the hook with nothing rendered, and there `$el` was `null`.

choices.text: `$el` is the first text of the template, `30 minutes`
choices.why: The text node is empty, not the paragraph's text: Vue adds it as a marker.

choices.text: Two roots, so `$el` is Vue's empty marker node
choices.why: Right. A component with several roots has no single element; a template ref names the one you mean.

choices.text:
Vue 3 reports the `nodeName` of a `

` as `#text`
choices.why:
A `

` reports `P`. The node here is not the paragraph at all.

prompt: Which Options API hooks have no `on…` partner in the Composition API? Choose all that apply.
hint: The top of `<script setup>` takes their place.

choices.text: `mounted`
choices.why: Its partner is `onMounted`.

choices.text: `created`
choices.why: Right. Top-level code in `<script setup>` runs at creation; there is no `onCreated`.

choices.text: `beforeUnmount`
choices.why: Its partner is `onBeforeUnmount`.

choices.text: `beforeCreate`
choices.why: Right. Like `created`, it is the top level of `<script setup>`.

choices.text: `activated`
choices.why: Its partner is `onActivated`, for a component kept alive.

prompt: Vue 2's `beforeDestroy` is called ___ in Vue 3, and a component still using the old name never runs that cleanup.
hint: The Composition partner is `onBeforeUnmount`; drop the `on`.

prompt: After an upgrade to Vue 3, the watcher `sessions(list) {}` stopped running when the code calls `this.sessions.push(…)`. What fixes it?
hint: Vue 2 watched arrays for mutation by default.

choices.text: Adding `immediate: true`
choices.why: `immediate` runs it once at the start; afterwards it is still shallow and a push still passes unseen.

choices.text: Moving it into `computed`, which follows arrays
choices.why: A computed derives a value; it is not where a side effect such as saving belongs, and it is not a watcher.

choices.text: `sessions: { handler(list) {}, deep: true }`
choices.why: Right. The option form is shallow too, unless `deep: true` is said.

choices.text: Calling `this.$forceUpdate()` after every push to the array
choices.why: That redraws the component and runs no watcher; the watcher is shallow and stays so.

prompt: What is the Options API's closest thing to `watchEffect`?
hint: It is a method on the instance, called from a hook.

choices.text: A `watchEffect` key inside the `watch` option
choices.why: The `watch` option takes sources by name; there is no `watchEffect` in the options.

choices.text: A `watch` entry with `immediate: true`
choices.why: That runs once at the start and then watches the one name it was given, not whatever it reads.

choices.text: A computed value that saves as a side effect
choices.why: A computed runs when something reads it, not when its sources change; a side effect there is a bug.

choices.text: `this.$watch(() => …, handler)` in `created`
choices.why: Right. It returns a stop function, and a component that needs more than that is a candidate for `setup()`.

prompt: Which `watch()` call is the Composition partner of the option `'session.minutes'(now) {}`?
hint: In the Composition API, a nested property is watched through a getter.

choices.text: `watch('session.minutes', (now) => {})`
choices.why: A string path is the option form's spelling; `watch()` takes a ref, a reactive object or a getter.

choices.text: `watch(() => session.value.minutes, (now) => {})`
choices.why: Right. The getter reads the one property, so the watcher runs when it changes.

choices.text: `watch(session, (now) => {}, { deep: true })`
choices.why: That runs on any change inside `session`, and `now` is the whole session rather than its minutes.

choices.text: `watch(session.value.minutes, (now) => {})`
choices.why: That passes the number the property holds at that moment, which nothing can track.

prompt: In `Mixins.vue`, why did the page show `course: course`?
hint: Look at the order of the `mixins` array.

choices.text: The first mixin's `describe` ran with the second one's `label`
choices.why: Then the page would read `progress: course`. Both names came from the same mixin.

choices.text: The component itself sets `label` to `'course'`
choices.why: `Mixins.vue` has no `data` of its own; every name on its `this` came from a mixin.

choices.text: Vue merges mixins in alphabetical order of their names
choices.why: The order is the array's, and `courseMixin` is listed second, which is why it won.

choices.text: The second mixin won both names
choices.why: Right. For `data` and `methods` the later one wins, and nothing warns.

prompt: A component and its mixins define the same options. Which statements describe how Vue 3 merges them? Choose all that apply.
hint: There are two rules, one for names and one for hooks.

choices.text: The component's own `methods` win over any mixin's
choices.why: Right. A mixin fills in; the component has the last word.

choices.text: Vue warns in development when two mixins define one method
choices.why: The transcript shows no warning: overwriting is how the merge works.

choices.text: Every `mounted` hook runs, the mixins' first
choices.why: Right. Hooks are the exception: they are all kept, in order.

choices.text: The first mixin in the list wins, and later ones only fill gaps
choices.why: It is the other way round: `courseMixin`, listed second, overwrote `progressMixin`.

choices.text: For `data`, the later mixin in the list wins
choices.why: Right. That is how `label` became `'course'`.

prompt: Which of the mixins' problems does `const { label: courseLabel } = useCourse()` deal with?
hint: What happens to a second `label` on the way in?

choices.text: Parameters: the rename hands `courseLabel` to the function
choices.why: Destructuring renames what came back; arguments go in the parentheses, as with `useWeek('2026-10-19')`.

choices.text: The collision, and the unclear origin with it
choices.why: Right. The caller names what it receives, so two `label`s cannot overwrite each other, and the line says where the name came from.

choices.text: Neither: a composable is merged into `this` the way a mixin is
choices.why: A composable is a function that returns values; nothing is merged, which is the point.

choices.text: Reactivity, which a mixin's `data` lacked
choices.why: A mixin's `data` is as reactive as the component's; the problems were all about names.

prompt: In `Mixing.vue`, where did `this.next` come from?
hint: Read the first option of the component.

choices.text: From `setup()`, which returned what `useWeek` gave it
choices.why: Right. What `setup()` returns joins `this`, beside `data` and `methods`.

choices.text: From `methods`, where Vue copies a composable's functions
choices.why: `methods` holds only `forward`. Nothing is copied: `setup()` returned `next` by name.

choices.text: From a mixin Vue builds out of `useWeek`
choices.why: Vue builds no mixin; the composable is called once, inside `setup()`.

choices.text: From `data`, into which `setup()` writes its values
choices.why: `data` holds only `moves`. What `setup()` returns sits on `this` beside it, not inside it.

prompt: What is `this` inside the `setup()` option?
hint: When does `setup()` run, relative to the other options?

choices.text: The props object, which is why props reach `this`
choices.why: Props arrive as `setup()`'s first argument instead; `this` is not involved.

choices.text: The component, with `data` and `methods` already on it
choices.why: Those options are set up after `setup()` returns; that is why it cannot read them through `this`.

choices.text: There is no `this` there
choices.why: Right. It runs before the instance's options are set up, and takes `props` as its first argument.

choices.text: The parent component that rendered it
choices.why: Nothing hands the parent to a child as `this`; inside `setup()` there is no `this` at all.

prompt: An old component keeps a timer in `data`, `mounted` and `beforeUnmount`, and you are asked to add a new composable to it. What is the first step the lesson gives?
hint: Step 1 of moving a component across.

choices.text: Change `<script>` to `<script setup>` and move every option across at once
choices.why: That is step 3, after nothing is left outside `setup()`. A component is moved, not rewritten in one go.

choices.text: Wrap the composable in a mixin, so that it fits the Options API
choices.why: That brings back the mixins' three problems; an Options component can call a composable from `setup()`.

choices.text: Add `setup()` and call the composable there, leaving the timer as it is
choices.why: Right. The rest of the options keep working, and the timer can move into `setup()` later as one concern.

choices.text: Move the timer's `data` into `setup()` first, and its hooks later
choices.why: A concern moves as a whole, state and hooks together, and nothing has to move for the new composable to be used.

prompt: Put the steps of moving an Options API component to `<script setup>` in order.
hint: The component keeps working after every step.
items: Add `setup()` and use a new composable from it
Move one concern's state, derived values, watcher and hooks into `setup()`
Repeat until nothing is left outside `setup()`
Change `<script>` to `<script setup>` and remove the `return`

prompt: Match each piece of Options API code to its Composition API partner.
hint: One line on the right has no partner on the left, and no partner in Vue either.

prompt: In the Options API, props, data, computed values and methods are merged onto ___, which is why a method written as an arrow cannot reach them.
hint: One keyword, the component instance as an option sees it.

prompt: A Vue 2 mixin `timerMixin`, used by six components, starts an interval in `mounted` and clears it in `beforeDestroy`. After the upgrade to Vue 3, removed components keep their intervals running. What is wrong?
hint: Two of the lesson's sections meet here: the hooks' names, and how a mixin's hooks are merged.

choices.text: Each component's own `beforeUnmount` overwrites the mixin's, as `methods` do
choices.why: Hooks are the exception to the merge: every one is kept and runs, the mixin's first.

choices.text: `beforeDestroy` is a Vue 2 name, and Vue 3 never calls it
choices.why: Right. Rename it `beforeUnmount`; and since the mixin has to be changed anyway, it is the moment to make it a composable.

choices.text: The watcher on the interval needs `deep: true` since Vue 3
choices.why: That was the arrays' upgrade problem. Nothing here is watched; a hook that never runs is the fault.

choices.text: The interval callback is an arrow, so `this` is lost
choices.why: An arrow inside a method keeps the method's `this`; that is the one place arrows are what you want.
